Nondelegation, History, and Original Meaning. Can the 
nondelegation doctrine be traced back historically to the founding era. As far 
as cases go, the early history seems thin. Cargo of the Bng Aurora (1813) was 
the first federal case to reference a nondelegation doctnne, and the oP^^on 
spoke to the issue for only a sentence or two. After Bng Aurora, the Court di 
not issue a clear holding on nondelegation until seventy-nine years later m 
Field V. Clark (1892). During the interim, the Court seems to have offered o^y 
dicta 2 and the dicta were no more specific than Chief Justice Marshy s 
comiAent in Wayman v. Southard: “The line has not been exactly cffawn which 
separates those important subjects which must be entirely regulated by the 
legislature itself, from those of less interest, in which a general provision may 
be made, and power given to those who are to act under such general provisions 
to fiU up the details.” 23 U.S. 1, 42-43 (1825). This may suggest a doctnne that 
turns upon a distinction between “important subjects” and those of less 
interest,” but that is not much guidance for deciding cases.
The core sources on original meaning—the text, drafting, and ratification 
of the federal and state constitutions, plus early legislative practice—have 
been the basis for an intense debate on whether the U.S. Constitution 
originally contained a nondelegation doctrine and, if so, what the original 
doctrine allows and prohibits. Some scholars argue that originalist sources do 
not support a nondelegation doctrine. E.g., Juhan Davis Mortenson & Nicholas 
Bagley, Delegation at the Founding, 121 Colum. L. Rev. 277 (2021). Other 
scholars argue they do. E.g., Aditya Bamzai, Alexander Hamilton, the 
Nondelegation Doctrine, and the Creation of the United States, 45 Harv. J.L. & 
Pub. Pol’y 795 (2022); Joseph Postell, Bureaucracy in America: The 
Administrative State’s Challenge to Constitutional Government 13—57 (2017), 
Tian Wurman, Nondelegation at the Founding, 130 Yale L.J. 1490 (2021).
The hterature turns up about a dozen assertions from various quarters of 
a constitutional limit on delegation from the start of the revolutionary crisis in 
1765 through ratification in 1788. Nicholas R. Parrillo, Supplemental Paper to: 
“A Critical Assessment of the Originalist Case Against Administrative 
Regulatory Power,” at 7—8, 36—49 (2021), https;//ssrn.com/abstract=3696902;
